@@132104181 <h> Theorising the Drivers of India 's Engagement in the Northern Sea Route <p> New Delhi is cognisant of the future viability of the Northern Sea Route , given the further thawing of the Arctic and the prospect of improved relations between Russia and other Arctic states over the long term . <p> New Delhi 's ambitions in the Arctic reflect a notable ideational shift in recent years . While India has long emphasised cooperation in science and climate research , its Arctic vision now carries a pronounced geo-economics dimension . This evolution stems from the accelerating thaw of Arctic ice and the growing prospect of year-round navigation along the Northern Sea Route ( with icebreaker assistance ) . Additionally , given Russia 's deteriorating relations with the West and the exit of Western investments , technology , and firms from the Russian Arctic due to sanctions , Moscow has welcomed the participation of Asian countries -- China and India -- in the Arctic . While Beijing has increased its presence in the Arctic over the last decade , India 's presence remains modest . Nevertheless , since the 2020s @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gained prominence in official discourse . Against this backdrop , tracing the drivers of India 's Arctic engagement , assessing the scope of its presence in the Russian Arctic , and examining the centrality of the NSR in New Delhi 's calculus warrant closer scrutiny . <h> India and the Arctic <p> New Delhi shares historic ties with the Arctic . In 1920 , India signed the Svalbard Treaty . Eighty-seven years later , in 2007 , New Delhi launched its first scientific expedition in the Arctic . In 2008 , India inaugurated its first Arctic outpost in Svalbard . The centrality of India 's Arctic policy places emphasis on strengthening cooperation in science and technology , economic and human development , climate change , Arctic governance , and enhancing connectivity . The growing importance of the Arctic in New Delhi 's calculus was reflected in its bid to join the Arctic Council , which was accepted in 2013 . Along with India , China , South Korea , Japan , and Singapore were granted observer status in the Arctic Council , which institutionalised Arctic governance on a global level @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Delhi articulated the region 's significance in its calculus , wherein , along with emboldening the existing pillars of engagement in the Arctic , two major shifts can be reflected in India 's approach . <p> First , the discourse around climate change in the Arctic is perceived through a domestic lens . New Delhi observes a synergy in the implications of climate change in the Arctic and Antarctic with that of the Himalayas . The latter is being positioned as a ' third pole ' , where the thawing of glaciers is leading to changes in weather conditions and monsoon patterns . Second , the strategy reflected a growing impetus towards strengthening economic and connectivity linkages with the Arctic regions . This shift can be attributed to the changes taking place in Russian Arctic geo-economics . Over the last decade , the development of energy and mineral extraction projects , Arctic ports , and strengthening connectivity nodes has been prioritised and can be reflected in key strategic documents , such as the 2020 Arctic Policy and the 2022 maritime doctrine . <p> Additionally , other neo-realist factors , such @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Arctic discourse , combined with the vacuum created by the exit of Western firms from the region , has contributed to growing Indian interest in strengthening engagement in the Arctic . In India 's calculus , enhancing cooperation in the Arctic has positive multiplier effects for the India-Russia partnership . This will build more equity for the Indian public and private sector , enhancing New Delhi 's presence in the Russian Arctic , especially in other sectors such as energy , mining , rare earth materials , and shipbuilding . <p> In 2021 , the Indian public sector 's investment in Russia , particularly in the energy and minerals segments , totalled $16 billion , indicative of a growing interest in strengthening bilateral energy cooperation . Since February 2022 , because of the rising discounts , New Delhi became the second largest importer of Russian crude , and bilateral trade exponentially increased , from $12 billion in 2021 to $66 billion in 2025 . While crude oil exports add up to a majority of the bilateral trade , non-oil trade subsequently began to increase in bilateral trade . Since the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaborating on the extraction of Arctic riches , energy resources , and rare earth materials . <h> Northern Sea Route <p> New Delhi 's interests in the NSR stem from the prospects of extending the Eastern Maritime Corridor -- connecting the eastern ports of India to Vladivostok and , in turn , connecting to the Russian North . New Delhi 's use of the NSR would enable circular connectivity with Russia along three directions : the existing route via Mumbai to St. Petersburg , the route via the Caucasus using the International North-South Transport Corridor , and , third , the Eastern Maritime Corridor . The NSR would complement these three routes not only in terms of navigation to Europe but also by enhancing connectivity between the Russian Arctic and Indian ports . Using the NSR from the Arctic ports via the EMC to reach Indian ports can reduce the number of shipping days . <p> In 2023 , Alexei Chekunkov , Russian Minister for the Development of the Far East and Arctic , visited India to discuss the transportation of goods via the NSR . In 2024 , during @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sides decided to set up a working group on the Northern Sea Route under the bilateral intergovernmental commission on trade , economic , scientific , technical , and cultural cooperation . During the plenary session of the working group , both sides discussed cargo transit targets , possible training for Indian seafarers in polar navigation , and joint projects for Arctic shipbuilding . With Russian port and shipbuilding facilities working on overdrive , Moscow has begun to offset the requirement of building non-nuclear icebreakers to third countries . Against this backdrop , last year , a $750 million MoU was concluded between Rosatom and the Government of India to build four non-nuclear icebreakers . <h> Challenges <p> Even with growing interest and the resultant institutionalisation of cooperation along the Northern Sea route , Indian investments in the Arctic have been negligible on the ground . Currently , India continues to import oil and LNG originating from the Russian Arctic , but external factors such as the threat of sanctions have influenced its engagement . For instance , last year , the Indian Oil Secretary announced that New Delhi would not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , even the case for using the NSR for the transit of Indian goods to Europe or North America is not commercially viable . This is due to constraints posed by structural realities and market forces . These include India 's low export-to-GDP ratio ( hovering around 20% ) with lesser focus on the manufacturing sector , which results in the formation of narrow comparative advantages for New Delhi in its export basket . Additionally , the high cost of transit , lack of ice-class vessels , and the challenge of insuring cargoes complicate transit , reducing the feasibility of the NSR . <p> Nevertheless , New Delhi is cognisant of the future viability of the NSR , given the further thawing of the Arctic and the prospect of improved relations between Russia and other Arctic states ( over the long term ) , which is why India is aiming to strengthen cooperation along the route . The vacuum created by the exit of the Western firms has created further avenues for joint collaboration in the Arctic . Furthermore , Moscow views New Delhi as a strategic partner in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ presence positively in the discourse of Arctic governance , which has been dysfunctional since Russia 's special military operation began . The current trends in Russia 's relations with the West are indicative of the further Easternisation of the Arctic , given the increased presence of Asian countries in the Arctic . Against this backdrop , President Vladimir Putin 's upcoming visit to India in early December is likely to place renewed emphasis on scaling up joint investments and enhancing India 's economic and scientific presence in the Russian Arctic . 
@@132106016 <p> Climate change itself acts as a threat multiplier , intensifying resource conflicts over water in Central Asia , arable land in Africa , and fish stocks in the warming Arctic -- Satyabrat Borah <p> Geopolitical conflict and global political instability have defined the early decades of the twenty-first century with an intensity not seen since the Cold War . The world is no longer shaped by a single bipolar rivalry or a unipolar moment of American dominance . Instead , it is caught in a web of overlapping crises , competing power centres , and accelerating technological change that together erode the foundations of the post-1945 international order . Great powers , middle powers , non-state actors , and transnational forces all pull in different directions , producing a landscape marked by proxy wars , economic coercion , frozen conflicts , and sudden eruptions of violence . Stability , once taken for granted in many regions , has become an exception rather than the rule . <p> The return of great-power competition lies at the heart of contemporary instability . The United States , though still the world 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has grown confident , wealthy , and assertive . Beijing 's Belt and Road Initiative , its militarisation of the South China Sea , and its relentless pressure on Taiwan signal a clear challenge to the American-led order in Asia . Washington has responded with trade restrictions , technology sanctions , and a network of new security arrangements such as AUKUS and the Quad . The rivalry is no longer confined to economics or diplomacy ; it increasingly carries the risk of direct military confrontation over Taiwan or disputed islands . Every large joint exercise , every new chip factory in Arizona or TSMC facility in Japan , and every freedom-of-navigation operation becomes a move on a chessboard where miscalculation could trigger catastrophe . <p> Russia 's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 marked the most dramatic rupture in European security since 1945 . Moscow 's attempt to annex its neighbour and overturn the post-Cold War settlement revealed both the fragility of deterrence and the limits of Western unity . The war has killed hundreds of thousands , displaced millions , and turned Ukraine into a laboratory for drone warfare @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ long accustomed to American protection , has been forced to confront its own military weakness and energy dependence . NATO has enlarged and rearmed , yet the continent remains vulnerable to hybrid attacks , sabotage of undersea cables , and nuclear sabre-rattling from the Kremlin . The conflict has also globalised : North Korean troops reportedly fight alongside Russians , Iranian drones darken Ukrainian skies , and Western missiles now strike inside Russia . What began as a regional war has become a worldwide confrontation by proxy . <p> In the Middle East , old certainties have collapsed . Many parts of Assam have already introduced alert mechanisms using mobile networks , drones , and watchtowers to inform villagers when herds are nearby . Strengthening these systems can help people prepare in advance , avoid conflict , and protect their crops . But what is multilateralism ? Why does it appear to stand at a crossroads today ? <p> This year 's G20 summit , held under the presidency of South Africa , has largely been seen as a rare victory for multilateralism . Notwithstanding the boycott and objections by the US , the G20 leaders adopted the summit declaration . <p> But how does the G20 declaration , ignoring US President Donald Trump 's warning and speculation about its future , reaffirm the idea of multilateralism ? What exactly is multilateralism , and how does it compare to bilateralism and unilateralism ? <h> What is multilateralism ? <p> In international relations , multilateralism is commonly used for any form of cooperation among states . The idea gained traction after WWI and was central to the formation of the League of Nations ( 1920 ) and the United Nations ( 1945 ) . <p> Thus @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Order or rules-based international order premised on liberal values like democracy , open market and shared rules . It stands in contrast to the realist tradition , where international order is defined as anarchic . <p> International relations scholar Robert O Keohane defined multilateralism as " the practice of co-ordinating national policies in groups of three or more states , through ad hoc arrangements or by means of institutions " . Other scholars like John Gerard Ruggie underlined the significance of " generalised principles " that coordinate relations among three or more states . <p> Thus , the idea of multilateralism is usually employed to refer to the interactions among states within institutionalised frameworks of cooperation such as international rules/law or the United Nations system . In other words , while working together through international organisations ( like the United Nations , World Trade Organisation ) , states abide by the rules/laws of international politics to propose common solutions to shared problems . <h> Multilateralism under strain ? <p> The growing integration of the world that followed the end of the Cold War sparked renewed interest in multilateralism . As @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ institutions to address global economic and political issues , such as trade , investment , climate change , conflicts , migration , etc . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> While such issues require international cooperation and solutions , multilateralism now appears to have reached a dead end . It is evident in the impasse created by great-power rivalries , de-globalisation , and populist nationalism , to name a few . <p> It underscores why countries like India have emphasised the need for multilateral reforms . At the same time , the G20 declaration addressing issues like climate change , debt sustainability , and just energy transitions reaffirmed the belief of leaders in multilateralism . <p> It stands in contrast with the idea of bilateralism and unilateralism . While bilateralism concerns relations or policies of joint action between two parties , unilateralism involves states acting independently , often promoting their national interests . @@132120208 <h> The desert region 's communities have relied on water reservoirs and wells built on a deep , practical knowledge of how soils behave in extreme aridity . <p> A man walks along with his camels in the sand dunes of Thar Desert at Sam village in India 's Rajasthan state on October 7 , 2021 . Sajjad Hussain / AFP <p> In the desert landscape of western Rajasthan , how communities use water has long depended on an intimate understanding of soil . <p> Water management systems such as khadeens , bavdi , beris , tankas , johads , naadi , naada and talab were built on a deep , practical knowledge of how soils behave in extreme aridity in the region characterised by low rainfall . Long before the language of " soil and moisture conservation " , " recharge " , " infiltration " entered policy vocabulary , localised systems of water harvesting were already in place . <p> Today , as India faces accelerating climate variability , land degradation , groundwater collapse and extreme heat , Rajasthan 's water systems are an urgent reminder and solution:soil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the evolution of Rajasthan 's soil-water wisdom , how it shaped community stewardship and the importance of reviving these systems offer lessons on climate resilience . <h> Soil power <p> Contemporary watershed interventions , involving measures such as bunds and planting trees , are often standardised across landscapes , but traditional systems in Rajasthan have been able to harness soil types to conserve water . Each structure is designed around specific soil textures , salinity levels , and slopes making the most of local geomorphology . <p> For example , it is understood that sand particles do not coalesce like clay , which cracks when hardened allowing moisture to escape . Sand particles stay separate as their porosity is high and do not harden or fissure . Moisture that seeps into the sand dunes does not escape , but instead percolates and collects . As Arati Kumar Rao notes in her book Marginlands , " The heart of the dune , a few feet deep , is a water storing miracle . " <p> The subcutaneous layer of the desert is gypsum , a mineral with a calcium base @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it from sinking deep into the water table , which is often salty . This water , which is neither surface water nor fossil water is called rejwani pani . Communities often depend on this for consumption . <p> Across Rajasthan 's arid districts , a range of water-harvesting systems are shaped by this understanding of local soils and rainfall patterns . <p> In Jaisalmer and Barmer , farmers construct khadeens , which are large earthen embankments built across drainage lines . These 6km-7km-wide systems slow runoff during rare rains , allowing silt to settle and moisture to percolate into deeper layers , sustaining crops long after rainfall . Surplus water flows sequentially from one khadeen to another , creating a cascading recharge system . <p> Alwar and Shekhawati districts rely on johads , which are small earthen reservoirs , primarily . By slowing runoff , they enhance silt deposition , enrich downstream fields , and recharge wells through steady percolation supported by vegetation and intact soil structure . <p> Western Rajasthan 's beris are traditional percolation wells that tap shallow aquifers . Constructed near ponds or within johad catchments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ filter water , while careful protection of surrounding soil ensures purity and continued recharge . <p> Tankas , or underground storage tanks fed by micro-catchments , are common in Bikaner , Phalodi , and Barmer . Tankas maximise runoff from small rainfall events for drinking water . Their compacted catchments and covered design reduce seepage and contamination , <h> Community practice <p> The sacred rule of the desert is that you do not deny anyone water . <p> Rajasthan 's water systems are embedded in local ethics and institutions , with each village being planned around water . Local grazing regulations prevent soil erosion around recharge zones . Village commons are protected to maintain vegetation that stabilises slopes with rules for silt removal , embankment repairs and seasonal maintenance . Digging and water conservation is a community effort , in which all would participate . <p> Oral traditions encode soil knowledge such as when to open spillways , where seepage indicates healthy recharge and how soil colour signals salinity . <p> Following these systems , each village has access to three types of water : <p> i ) palar pani @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ aagor , or catchment <p> ii ) rejwani pani , which is percolated , or capillary water siphoned by beris <p> iii ) patali pani , or the deep water table reached by the wells <p> This way , no single source will get overused and run dry . <p> Which water gets used when is governed by a natural cycle : once the lakes dry up , beris come into play in the deepest part of the Thar where there is no underlying gypsum layer that can hold water , making the well a lifeline . <p> Urbanisation and land-use change have severed communities from the landscapes that once sustained them . The standardisation of watershed techniques affects water and soil if not done appropriately . The resulting loss of traditional knowledge means that fewer people understand soil properties that make these systems work . <p> Strengthening existing localised and traditional forms of watershed management could do wonders for preventing water scarcity . <h> Climate resilience , indigenous knowledge <p> As climate change intensifies drought cycles and heat stress , soil is the frontline of resilience . Healthy soils @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and recharge aquifers . They also enhance water quality through natural filtration while supporting biodiversity that stabilises ecosystems . In arid areas , soil determines whether water survives long enough for people and livestock to access it . In Rajasthan , soil conservation is water security . <p> On World Soil Day , Rajasthan 's water systems show that soil health is integral to building climate resilience . @@132121965 <h> Climate change and environmental pollution is one of the most pressing environmental challenges affecting ecosystems , agriculture and animal health <p> From the recent past certain issues related to health , ecosystems and environment have emerged . These issues if not pondered upon and acted judiciously and well in time may harm our future generations and in broader sense the whole ecosystem , the environment and the health of all living beings in a " One Health Context " . <p> Many of these issues also have spiritual , cultural and social implications as well . The use of drugs in veterinary practice has become a cause of public health concern as these residues may impose a health risk to consumers . <p> The presence of drug residues in foods like milk and meat may be the result of various factors like failure to observe the withdrawl and withholding periods , extra label use of drugs , faulty or inappropriate dosage of drugs . The development of antimicrobial resistance is neither an unexpected nor a novel problem . It is , however , becoming alarming due to the frequency with which new emerging resistant phenotypes are developing among many bacterial pathogens and even commensal organisms . <p> The indiscriminate use of drugs and chemicals , particularly antimicrobials , in agriculture and livestock has become a significant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ livestock farming , antibiotics are commonly used not only to treat diseases but also for growth promotion and preventive purposes . This overuse and misuse create selective pressure that allows resistant bacteria to survive and multiply . <p> These resistant bacteria , along with antibiotic residues , can enter the food chain through meat , milk , eggs , and even crops fertilized with contaminated manure , posing a direct threat to human health . Such practices also reduce the effectiveness of antibiotics essential for treating human infections , contributing to the global problem of antimicrobial resistance ( AMR ) . Clinicians need to be more reliable on data from in-vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing and emphasize the importance of the diagnostic laboratory in veterinary practice . <p> Beyond human health , antimicrobial residues and chemicals from agriculture have serious ecological impacts . When excreted into the environment through animal waste , these substances persist in soil and water , disrupting microbial communities and promoting the spread of resistance genes among environmental bacteria . <p> This alteration in microbial ecology can affect nutrient cycling , soil fertility , and overall ecosystem @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ chain , affecting wildlife and ultimately creating a feedback loop that exacerbates resistance in both humans and animals . <p> Addressing these issues requires a holistic One Health approach that integrates human , animal and environmental health . Strategies include strict regulation and monitoring of antimicrobial use in farming , adopting alternatives like vaccines and probiotics , improving hygiene and farm management practices and raising awareness among farmers and stakeholders . Sustainable antimicrobial stewardship , along with research into new therapeutic options , is essential to mitigate the spread of resistance , safeguard public health and maintain the integrity of ecosystems . <p> Pesticides and Chemicals in plant foods <p> Synthetic pesticides used for plant based food production although enhance crop productivity , suppress pest population and ensure post harvest presentation but has raised concerns regarding environmental integrity , human health and long term agricultural sustainability when used over an extended period of time . The compounds such as organophosphates and carbamates contaminate water sources , influence soil microbiota contributing to bioaccumulation over different trophic levels . <p> The exposure to these chemicals as per study is associated with endocrine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in children and pregnant individuals hence more and more emphasis should be laid on organic farming , better pest management and use of natural manures so that both human , animal and environmental health are safeguarded . <p> Climatic changes and environmental pollution <p> The influence of environmental pollution and climate change on veterinary and related industries has become a significant concern in recent years . Environmental hazards affecting veterinary and allied sectors can arise in multiple ways including health risks , ecological disruptions and habitat degradation . Various sources of pollution such as air , soil , water and noise contribute to these issues causing both direct and indirect impacts . <p> In the livestock direct effects include respiratory disorders , exposure to toxins and behavioral changes in animals , while indirect consequences may involve disruptions in the food chain , declining reproductive health , and an increased prevalence of zoonotic diseases . <p> Degraded soil quality directly impacts animal health . Pollutants absorbed by forage crops or leached into groundwater result in the accumulation of harmful substances in animal feed and water supplies . This can lead to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Heavy metal toxicity is a frequent concern in contaminated regions , while pesticide residues pose severe health risks to both terrestrial and aquatic animals . Once these contaminants seep into the soil , they can enter the food chain , jeopardizing human health and increasing the prevalence of associated diseases . <p> More than 60% of India 's GDP comes from cities , with major economic hubs like Bangalore and Mumbai serving as industrial centers . Urban regions are hubs for cultural innovation , entrepreneurship and research . Infrastructure such as metro systems , airports and cutting-edge communication networks are built here . Urban life may give more amenities , as well as more entertainment and aesthetically pleasing environment . <p> Urbanization has adverse effects also . Un-treated urban garbage for instance harms rivers , lakes , ponds and streams . Urban sprawl is the cause of deforestation and the loss of green cover . More than 65 million Indians endure substandard housing and sanitation conditions in slums . The gap between the wealthiest in cities and the destitute in rural areas is growing as a result of urbanization @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ financial losses . As a result of growing urbanization , cities like Chennai and Jaipur have had serious water issues . <p> With little capacity for recycling or disposal , cities produce more than 1.5 lakh metric tons of waste per day , endangering ecosystems and the environment . Because of inadequate drainage infrastructure , flooding during the monsoon season increases urban vulnerabilities . Delhi 's biggest problem is still air pollution , which is mostly caused by industrial activity and vehicle emissions . There is also a severe water shortage in the city , particularly in the summer . <p> One of the most pressing concerns of rapid urbanization is the conversion of agricultural land for urban development . Expanding cities encroach upon fertile lands leading to a decline in cultivable areas . According to studies millions of hectares of farmland are lost to urban expansion annually , threatening food security . Urbanization also causes immense pressure on natural resources . <p> The increasing demand for water in cities often reduces availability for irrigation . Industrial pollution , improper waste disposal and urban runoff further contaminate water bodies affecting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ loss of biodiversity and soil degradation caused by urbanization leads to environmental imbalances . The replacement of green landscapes with concrete structures alter local climatic conditions making agriculture more vulnerable to extreme weather events such as heat waves and erratic rainfall patterns . <p> Industrialization and Urbanization pose pathetic influences on livestock and agriculture causing structural disruptions which in turn affect their ecological stability , productivity and long term viability . The urbanization has converted fertile lands into commercial and residential lands shrinking pastoral lands and fragmenting traditional farming landscapes . <p> The term emerging diseases is defined by the WHO , FAO as newly recognized or evolved pathogen , which is a recent one or it has occurred previously , but which shows an increase in its incidence or expansion in the geographic area regarding the number of hosts and vectors . These emerging diseases have a devastating impact on both livestock and poultry , resulting in significant loss and posing serious threat to public health . <p> Emerging and re-emerging diseases in livestock are infections that either appear for the first time in a population or reappear after @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ result from changes in the environment , climate , livestock management practices , or the introduction of pathogens into new regions through trade and animal movement . Re-emerging diseases , on the other hand , are infections that were previously controlled but have resurfaced due to factors like drug resistance , lapses in vaccination , or changes in host susceptibility . <p> These diseases pose serious challenges to the livestock sector , leading to reduced productivity , high mortality , and significant economic losses for farmers and the agricultural economy . They can also threaten food security by affecting the availability of milk , meat , and other animal products . Some diseases may have zoonotic potential , meaning they can be transmitted to humans , thereby posing public health risks . <p> Deforestation and desertification and its influence on livestock and agriculture : Deforestation and desertification are two of the most pressing environmental issues affecting livestock production globally . Deforestation , the large-scale removal of forests for agriculture , urbanization , or industrial purposes , leads to the loss of natural grazing lands , fodder plants , and water @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of rangelands but also disrupts local ecosystems , affecting soil fertility , microclimate and biodiversity , which are all essential for maintaining healthy livestock populations . When forests are cleared , exposed soils are more prone to erosion , nutrient depletion and desertification , creating a cascade of negative effects on livestock productivity . <p> Desertification , defined as the degradation of arid , semi-arid , and dry sub-humid lands , is accelerated by overgrazing , unsustainable agricultural practices and climate change . It results in the loss of vegetation cover , reduction in soil moisture and decreased availability of natural pastures . Livestock in affected areas face nutritional stress due to limited fodder and water resources , making them more susceptible to diseases and mortality . In addition , changes in land cover and climate can alter the distribution of pests and disease vectors , further threatening livestock health . <p> The economic impact of deforestation and desertification is significant . Reduced livestock productivity , higher mortality rates and declining quality of animal products directly affect the livelihoods of pastoral communities , especially in semi-arid and arid regions of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ socio-economic consequences extend to food security , market dynamics and rural economies that heavily rely on livestock . <p> Addressing these challenges requires integrated and sustainable land management approaches . Managed grazing systems , reforestation programs , soil conservation techniques and water resource management can help restore degraded lands and maintain livestock productivity . The use of modern tools like Geographic Information Systems ( GIS ) and remote sensing enables the monitoring of land degradation , early identification of vulnerable areas , and informed decision-making for interventions . Additionally , raising awareness among farmers about sustainable grazing , pasture rotation and environmental stewardship is critical . <p> Ultimately , balancing livestock and agricultural production with human health and environmental conservation is essential for long-term sustainability . Collaborative efforts between administrators , academicians , agriculturists , veterinarians , ecologists , policymakers , farmers and local communities can create resilient livestock and agricultural systems that thrive even in regions vulnerable to deforestation and desertification . @@132134279 <h> India 's Path to Peace : A Scriptural Perspective <h> Share : <p> India , often referred to as the land of spirituality and diversity , has been a cradle of civilizations , religions , and philosophies for millennia . Its rich tapestry of cultures , languages , and faiths has coexisted , albeit with occasional tensions , under the overarching ethos of unity in diversity . This paper explores how India , as a land of believers , can harness its spiritual and scriptural heritage to build a society rooted in peace , harmony , and justice . <p> Drawing from the teachings of Hinduism , Christianity , and Islam , this paper argues that the ethical and moral frameworks embedded in these traditions provide a robust foundation for fostering peace in a pluralistic society like India . The scriptures , philosophies , and values of these three major religions offer a shared vision for peace , compassion , and coexistence . India 's greatest wealth is her spirituality . This wealth can be leveraged to promote peace , tolerance , and understanding among India 's diverse communities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of India , we can foster a culture of peace , promote interfaith understanding , and address social and economic inequalities . The values of non-violence , compassion , and forgiveness that are inherent in these traditions can help create a culture of peace that transcends religious and cultural boundaries . Furthermore , exploring the commonalities and shared values among Hinduism , Christianity , and Islam can promote interfaith understanding and cooperation . Ultimately , drawing from the teachings of these traditions can help address social and economic inequalities , promoting justice and fairness for all . <p> This paper aims to provide a framework for harnessing India 's spiritual and scriptural heritage to build a more peaceful , harmonious , and just society . <p> 1 . Ethical Foundations of Peace in Hinduism , Christianity , and Islam <p> The concept of dharma , often translated as righteousness , duty , or moral law , lies at the heart of Hinduism . It is the ethical and spiritual foundation that upholds the individual , society , and the cosmos . Dharma is not a rigid set of rules but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and circumstance . It encompasses moral duty , justice , and the ethical order that sustains the harmony of the universe . In the Bhagavad Gita , one of Hinduism 's most revered texts , Lord Krishna declares His divine mission to restore dharma whenever it declines : " Whenever there is a decline of righteousness and an increase in unrighteousness , O Arjuna , I manifest Myself to protect the virtuous , to annihilate the wicked , and to re-establish dharma " ( Bhagavad Gita 4.7-8 ) . This profound statement underscores the cyclical nature of dharma and its restoration as a divine imperative . <p> Krishna 's teachings in the Bhagavad Gita provide a comprehensive guide to living a life aligned with dharma . He outlines 26 qualities of a virtuous individual , including mercy , truthfulness , equanimity , and peacefulness . These qualities are not merely personal virtues but are essential for fostering a harmonious society . For instance , truthfulness ( satya ) ensures trust and integrity in relationships , while equanimity ( samatva ) cultivates inner peace and resilience in the face of life @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ karuna ) encourage empathy and kindness , bridging divides and fostering unity . Together , these virtues form the bedrock of a society where individuals coexist in mutual respect and cooperation . <p> The pursuit of harmony in Hinduism extends beyond human relationships to encompass all of creation . The Vedic call for universal peace , encapsulated in the prayer " Loka samastha sukhino bhavantu " ( May all beings everywhere be happy ) , reflects Hinduism 's inclusive vision of peace . This prayer is not limited to humans but includes all living beings , emphasizing the interconnectedness of life . The concept of ahimsa ( non-violence ) further reinforces this vision , advocating for a lifestyle that minimizes harm to others and the environment . Ahimsa is not merely the absence of physical violence but also the avoidance of harmful thoughts , words , and actions . It is a proactive commitment to compassion and respect for all life forms . <p> Hinduism 's emphasis on dharma and harmony is deeply rooted in its understanding of the cosmos . According to Hindu philosophy , the universe is a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ expression of the same ultimate reality ( Brahman ) . This worldview fosters a sense of unity and interdependence , encouraging individuals to see themselves as part of a larger whole . The practice of yoga , which means " union , " is a practical means of realizing this unity . Through physical postures ( asanas ) , breath control ( pranayama ) , and meditation ( dhyana ) , yoga helps individuals harmonize their body , mind , and spirit , aligning themselves with the cosmic order . <p> The pursuit of harmony in Hinduism is also reflected in its rituals and festivals . These practices are not merely cultural expressions but are designed to align individuals with the rhythms of nature and the divine . For example , the festival of Diwali , the festival of lights , symbolizes the triumph of light over darkness , knowledge over ignorance , and good over evil . It is a time for families and communities to come together , fostering social cohesion and shared joy . Similarly , the practice of puja ( worship ) involves offering flowers , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and reverence for the divine presence in all aspects of life . These rituals serve as reminders of the interconnectedness of all beings and the importance of living in harmony with the cosmos . <p> Hinduism 's vision of harmony is not limited to the individual or society but extends to the relationship between humanity and nature . The ancient texts , such as the Vedas and Upanishads , emphasize the sacredness of the natural world . Rivers , mountains , trees , and animals are revered as manifestations of the divine , and their protection is considered a moral duty . The concept of ' Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam ' ( the world is one family ) encapsulates this holistic vision , urging individuals to treat the earth and all its inhabitants with care and respect . The mantra from the Mahanarayana Upanishad , " Yatra vishvam bhavati eka nidam , " inspires a profound sense of unity , encouraging us to envision the world as a single , harmonious home . This perspective encompasses all living beings , from the smallest insects to the most evolved humans , as part @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , our desire for the well-being of all should extend to our planet , nature , all nations , and the entire human family . In a world facing environmental crises , this ancient wisdom offers a timely reminder of the need for sustainable living and ecological balance . <p> The pursuit of dharma and harmony in Hinduism is not without its challenges . In a world marked by diversity and conflict , the principles of dharma can sometimes seem abstract or difficult to apply . However , Hinduism provides practical tools for navigating these challenges . The practice of seva ( selfless service ) encourages individuals to contribute to the well-being of others without expecting anything in return . By serving others , individuals transcend their ego and experience a deeper sense of connection and purpose . Similarly , the practice of forgiveness ( kshama ) helps individuals let go of resentment and anger , fostering inner peace and reconciliation . <p> Hinduism 's emphasis on dharma and the pursuit of harmony offers a profound and timeless vision for living a meaningful and ethical life . The Indian Legacy of Pluralism and Coexistence <p> India 's history is a rich tapestry woven with threads of diverse cultures , religions , and philosophies , each contributing to the vibrant mosaic of its civilization . This legacy of pluralism and coexistence is deeply rooted in the ancient Indian ideal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of nation , creed , and caste dissolve , and humanity is united in a shared bond of kinship . This principle , which transcends geographical , cultural , and religious boundaries , reflects the inclusive ethos of Indian civilization . It is a call to recognize the inherent unity of all humanity , despite apparent differences . The Vedas , Upanishads , and other sacred texts of India have long emphasized this unity amidst diversity . For instance , the Rig Veda proclaims : " Let us have concord with our own people , and concord with people who are strangers to us ... May we unite in our minds , unite in our purposes , and not fight against the divine spirit within us " ( Atharva Veda 7.52.1-2 ) . This verse encapsulates the spirit of harmony and mutual respect that has been a hallmark of Indian thought for millennia . <p> The Indian tradition of pluralism is not merely a philosophical ideal but a lived reality . Throughout its history , India has been a sanctuary for various religious and cultural traditions , from Hinduism , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and Zoroastrianism . The ancient edicts of Emperor Ashoka , who ruled in the 3rd century BCE , exemplify this commitment to coexistence . Ashoka , after embracing Buddhism , promoted principles of non-violence ( ahimsa ) , compassion , and respect for all religious traditions . His rock edicts declare : " All religions should reside everywhere , for all of them desire self-control and purity of heart " ( Rock Edict XII ) . This message of tolerance and mutual respect remains a cornerstone of India 's cultural heritage . <p> The Upanishads , which form the philosophical foundation of Hinduism , further reinforce the idea of unity in diversity . The famous dictum Tat Tvam Asi ( Thou art That ) from the Chandogya Upanishad ( 6.8.7 ) teaches that the essence of the individual self ( atman ) is identical to the universal reality ( Brahman ) . This profound insight underscores the interconnectedness of all beings and serves as a spiritual basis for pluralism . Similarly , the Bhagavad Gita , a text revered by millions , emphasizes the importance of seeing the divine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ all beings , and all beings in the Self , sees truly " ( 6.29 ) . This vision of universal oneness encourages individuals to transcend narrow identities and embrace a broader sense of kinship with all life . <p> In modern times , figures like Swami Vivekananda have championed India 's legacy of pluralism and coexistence on the global stage . In his famous 1893 speech at the Parliament of the World 's Religions in Chicago , Vivekananda declared : " I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance . We believe not only in universal toleration but we accept all religions as true . " This statement , rooted in the teachings of the Vedanta philosophy , reflects the essence of India 's spiritual heritage . Vivekananda 's message was not merely about tolerance but about celebrating the diversity of religious paths as different expressions of the same ultimate truth . His words continue to inspire millions , reminding the world of the importance of dialogue , understanding , and mutual respect . <p> The Indian tradition of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and architecture , which often blend elements from different cultures and religions . For example , the Sufi tradition in India , with its emphasis on love and devotion , has deeply influenced Indian music , poetry , and spirituality . The poetry of Kabir , a 15th-century mystic , exemplifies this syncretic spirit . Kabir , who drew from both Hindu and Islamic traditions , wrote : " The river is one , though the banks are different . " His verses celebrate the unity of all spiritual paths and critique the divisions created by dogma and ritual . Similarly , the architectural marvels of India , such as the Taj Mahal and the Golden Temple , stand as symbols of the country 's ability to harmonize diverse cultural influences into a cohesive whole . <p> India 's legacy of pluralism and coexistence is not without challenges . The country has faced periods of conflict and division , often fuelled by political , social , or economic factors . The Indian Constitution , adopted in 1950 , enshrines the principles of secularism , equality , and fraternity , reflecting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the freedom of religion , affirming that " all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess , practice , and propagate religion . In a world grappling with polarization and conflict , the concept of a global family and shared nest offers a compelling reminder of our collective humanity . The wisdom of the Vedas , Upanishads , and other sacred texts , complemented by the inspiring examples of visionaries like Ashoka ( BCE 304-232 ) , Kabir ( 1398-1518 ) , and Vivekananda ( 1863-1902 ) , highlights that diversity can be a powerful catalyst for growth , strength , and enrichment , rather than division . By embracing pluralism and coexistence , societies can cultivate deeper understanding , cooperation , and peace , ultimately fostering a more harmonious world . <p> India 's journey toward pluralism and coexistence is ongoing , requiring constant effort and vigilance . I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house as freely as possible . " ( Young India , June 1 , 1921 ) This vision of openness and inclusivity is at the heart of India 's legacy and serves as a guiding light for the future . <p> The Indian legacy of pluralism and coexistence is a testament to the enduring power of unity in diversity . Challenges to Peace in Contemporary India <p> India , with its rich spiritual heritage and legacy of pluralism , has long been a beacon of coexistence and harmony . However , the nation faces significant challenges to peace in the contemporary era , which threaten to undermine its social fabric and collective well-being . These challenges are multifaceted , rooted in political , social , economic , and environmental issues , and they demand urgent attention and thoughtful solutions . <p> One of the most pressing challenges is the rise of identity-based politics , which often exploits divisions along the lines of caste , religion , and ethnicity . While India 's diversity has historically been a source of strength , it has also been manipulated for political @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Politicians and groups sometimes use divisive rhetoric to mobilize support , creating an " us versus them " mentality that deepens societal fractures . This politicization of identity not only erodes trust between communities but also distracts from pressing issues such as development , education , and healthcare . The consequences of such divisive politics are evident in incidents of communal violence , which leave lasting scars on the nation 's social fabric . Addressing this challenge requires a renewed commitment to the principles of unity and inclusivity that have long been central to India 's ethos . <p> Another significant challenge is the proliferation of misinformation and hate speech , particularly on social media platforms . While the internet has democratized access to information and enabled free expression , it has also become a breeding ground for falsehoods and inflammatory content . Misinformation spreads rapidly , often fuelling fear , suspicion , and hostility between communities . Hate speech , whether directed at religious , caste , or ethnic groups , exacerbates existing tensions and can incite violence . The anonymity and reach of social media make it difficult @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these platforms often prioritize sensational content , further amplifying divisive narratives . Combating this issue requires a multi-pronged approach , including stricter regulation of online content , public awareness campaigns to promote media literacy , and efforts to foster a culture of responsible communication . <p> Economic inequality is another major obstacle to peace in contemporary India . Despite significant economic growth in recent decades , the benefits of development have not been evenly distributed . A large portion of the population continues to live in poverty , lacking access to basic necessities such as clean water , healthcare , and education . This disparity exacerbates social tensions , as marginalized groups feel excluded from the opportunities and resources available to others . Economic inequality often intersects with other forms of discrimination , such as caste and gender , creating a cycle of disadvantage and resentment . Addressing this challenge requires inclusive policies that prioritize the needs of the most vulnerable , as well as efforts to create equitable opportunities for all . <p> Environmental degradation is another critical challenge that threatens peace and stability in India . The country @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , air pollution , deforestation , and soil degradation . These issues not only harm the environment but also have severe social and economic consequences . For instance , water scarcity can lead to conflicts between communities , while air pollution contributes to health problems and reduces quality of life . Climate change exacerbates these challenges , increasing the frequency and intensity of natural disasters such as floods and droughts . The impact of environmental degradation is particularly severe for marginalized communities , who often depend on natural resources for their livelihoods . Addressing this issue requires sustainable development practices , stronger environmental regulations , and greater public awareness of the importance of conservation . Initiatives such as the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan ( Clean India Mission ) and the National Solar Mission are positive steps , but a more comprehensive and coordinated approach is needed to tackle the scale of the problem . <p> These challenges highlight the need for a renewed commitment to the ethical and spiritual values that have historically sustained Indian society . These values emphasize the importance of unity , compassion , and respect for all life , providing a moral framework for addressing the root causes of conflict and division . <p> Education also plays a crucial role in fostering peace and social cohesion . By promoting critical thinking , empathy , and a sense of shared responsibility , education can help counter the forces of division and hatred . Schools and universities should incorporate lessons on India 's pluralistic heritage , as well as the importance of tolerance and mutual respect . Civil society organizations , religious leaders , and community groups also have a vital role to play in promoting dialogue and understanding between different groups . <p> Ultimately , building a peaceful and inclusive India requires collective effort and a shared vision for the future . It calls for political leaders to prioritize the common good over narrow interests , for citizens to reject divisive narratives and embrace their shared humanity , and for policymakers to address the structural inequalities that fuel social tensions . For what Marxian thinking offers in this regard , we must turn to Saito 's deep dive into the ecological Marx he discovered participating in a global project to uncover Marx 's lesser known @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , <p> " Degrowth through Marx ? Are you crazy ? I began writing this book well aware that I 'd face this sort of disbelieving response from all quarters . " <p> That is because the Marx most of us know is the Marx who boldly proclaimed the industrial revolution taking place in Western Europe when he wrote in the mid-19th century was needed to realize his vision of communism . It is the Marx of productivism , Saito writes . The capitalist bourgeois in revolutionizing production would accumulate so much wealth unto themselves that they would impoverish the working class , which would as a result seize the means of production and place them under direct worker management . <p> The fact this did n't happen , and that the actual Marxian revolutions that did take place in Russia and China were in agrarian societies and more caused by the upheavals of war , are taken as a refutation of Marx . Labor unions and progressive reforms resulted in some redistribution of income in the west , while the Soviet and Chinese regimes became massive state capitalisms under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ critical of these regimes for just these reasons . <p> Saito instead looks to a different Marx , one whose ecological leanings emerged more in the latter days of his life . He draws heavily from a global project to surface and publish the complete writings of Marx and his partner , Friedrich Engels , including Marx 's extensive , previously unpublished notes . Marx at the time of his death had not completed the second and third volume of Capital , leaving that to Engels . Saito speculates that Marx was having difficulty integrating his new insights , which Engels did not fully capture . <p> Writing the first volume , Marx had already been influenced by Justus von Liebig , a German chemist who concluded that commercial agriculture robbed the soil . Modern sewage treatment broke the older cycle of returning human wastes to fertilize it . Increased pressure to produce for profit intensified depletion . Commercial agriculture displaced these costs through use of fertilizers , such as the bird guano collected from islands in Marx 's day . @@132142733 <p> The relationship between China and India stands today as one of the most significant , delicate , and closely watched geopolitical engagements of the modern era . These two ancient civilisations , rising global powers , and neighbouring giants carry not only centuries of history but also the weight of present-day ambitions that frequently pull them towards rivalry rather than cooperation . In an age where economic aspirations , military strategies , technological competition , and regional influence intertwine with domestic politics and national pride , the China -- India equation transforms into a theatre of subtle diplomacy , restrained tension , and uneasy coexistence . The political issue between these two countries is not an isolated dispute but a deeply layered narrative shaped by geography , memory , perception , and the ever-shifting aspirations of two nations determined to define their place in the twenty-first century . <p> The story begins at the point where territorial ambiguity became political mistrust . These conflicting perceptions create a fragile environment where mistrust becomes the default state , and even small deviations in routine military activity risk triggering wider consequences . <p> The memory of the 1962 war has not faded from India 's political and public consciousness . It influences how the nation views China 's intentions and shapes the strategic mindset of every government that comes to power in New Delhi . For China , the war is a historical chapter that reinforces its narrative of territorial integrity and national revival . This asymmetry in historical memory creates different emotional registers on both sides . India carries caution and unresolved trauma ; China projects confidence and strategic assertiveness . These emotional undercurrents influence policy decisions , diplomatic language , and the broader domestic debate whenever China and India are mentioned in political @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moment in modern China -- India relations . China increased military presence along strategic points , India responded with rapid troop mobilisation , and the Himalayan frontier transformed into an arena of hardened postures and long-term deployments . Roads , tunnels , bridges , surveillance systems , and airlift capacities expanded at unprecedented speed , signalling that neither country intends to retreat from this new state of constant preparedness . <p> The political leadership of both countries faces the challenge of balancing domestic expectations with international responsibility . Edited excerpts : <p> Global geo-economic shifts have become more frequent . How should CEOs , whether leading global or local firms , navigate this new landscape ? <p> It 's a significant challenge , especially for CEOs in the West who have spent most of their careers in a world that felt stable and predictable . Suddenly , the terrain has shifted . Leaders now recognize that we 're not returning to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ precede economics . The first questions are now : Can I operate there ? Am I welcome ? Who will support me if things go wrong ? This shift affects capital allocation , risk management and strategy . It means spreading bets more widely , prioritising reliability over efficiency , and building organisations that can adapt quickly . The winners in this environment will be those who can consistently meet customer needs despite political or economic turbulence , who move from efficiency driven models to agility and resilience driven ones . <p> Are political risks , protectionism and geo-economic tensions now bigger concerns than economic cycles ? <p> My bigger worry is n't tariffs or protectionism , though those matter . It 's the erosion of global leadership and governance . Since World War II , the US , working through international institutions , has provided a framework for coordinated responses to global challenges . That system is weakening . Without strong leadership-whether from the US or others-we risk losing the ability to respond to issues like climate change or global crises effectively . China is providing some leadership in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has been absent on major geopolitical issues like Gaza or Ukraine . So , the concern is not just the economic cycle ; it 's the absence of a coherent global response to global problems . <h> Live Events <p> How are Indian corporate leaders placed to deal with such challenges vis-a-vis their global peers ? <p> Indian leaders have long operated in an environment marked by uncertainty-frequent policy shifts , supply-chain disruptions , regulatory changes and macro volatility . The new global paradigm feels more familiar to Indian CEOs than for many of their peers in the West . <p> With AI emerging as a major force , how are corporate leaders dealing with the shift ? <p> Every CEO I speak to believes AI is transformative . The debate is not whether it will reshape industries , but how dramatically . Many expect major productivity gains and automation . Companies are investing heavily in upskilling and AI literacy so employees can use these tools effectively . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at scale -especially in customer service , content generation and operations . A CEO can not move quickly or decisively without a board that understands the environment and supports change . But boards are often the most risk-averse part of the system , which can create friction . @@132182033 <h> The FAO -- WHO report warns that chemical contaminants from natural toxins to industrial pollutants and PFAS are increasingly entering food through irrigation , livestock water and aquaculture as water scarcity drives greater use of alternative water sources . It identifies eleven high-risk contaminants and urges stronger One Health -- based regulation , monitoring and water treatment to safeguard global food safety . <p> The FAO and WHO 's 2025 report on chemical water quality in agrifood systems , developed with key scientific contributions from the University of Campinas , the National Institute of Environmental Studies Japan , Cawthron Institute New Zealand , the University of East Anglia , the University of Alabama , the University of Nairobi , JEFCS UK , Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada and Chung-Ang University , delivers a clear alarm : food safety can no longer be separated from water safety . As agriculture draws more than 70 percent of global freshwater , rising demand , climate disruption and the growing dependence on non-conventional water sources are allowing chemical contaminants , many previously overlooked , to slip into the food supply through irrigation , livestock @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ How Chemicals Move From Water to Food <p> FAO and WHO map out several pathways by which contaminants enter the human diet . Livestock absorb chemicals directly through drinking water , allowing pollutants to accumulate in muscle , organs , milk or eggs . Fish and shellfish , constantly immersed , bioaccumulate both dissolved and particle-bound contaminants , sometimes at levels far exceeding those in the water itself . Crops absorb soluble contaminants from soil or accumulate residues from foliar irrigation , and some pharmaceuticals , carbamazepine being a notable example , survive wastewater treatment and appear in vegetables irrigated with treated effluent . Post-harvest washing with contaminated water allows toxins to bypass biological barriers entirely and adhere directly to food surfaces . These pathways highlight that water quality is not merely an environmental issue but a direct food safety concern . <h> The Chemicals of Highest Concern <p> By comparing contamination levels in food with health-based guidance values , the report identifies eleven contaminants of greatest concern , those for which dietary exposure via water sources alone may exceed or approach toxic thresholds . They include arsenic , cadmium @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of which are potent geogenic toxicants associated with chronic disease ; the cyanobacterial toxins microcystins , cylindrospermopsins , saxitoxins and anatoxin-a , which can cause severe acute poisoning ; and the persistent PFAS chemicals PFOA and PFOS , which accumulate in the environment and human bodies . Medium-priority contaminants such as carbamazepine , perchlorate , nickel , phthalates and PCBs may not exceed limits individually but contribute significantly to cumulative dietary exposure . The report notes that climate change is multiplying the risks , fueling harmful algal blooms , concentrating metals during droughts , and mobilizing industrial contaminants during floods.

UNEP 's report provides a severe account of the missed pledges and false statements . Three points are essential to grasp : <p> Developing countries will require between $310 billion and $365 billion per year by 2035 for climate adaptation alone ( setting aside mitigation as well as loss and damage ) . If inflation is taken at 3 percent per year , then real adaptation needs will reach between $440 billion and $520 billion annually by 2035 . <p> In 2023 adaptation finance flows from developed to developing countries were just $26 billion , less than in 2022 , and 58 percent of the money came through debt instruments and not through grants -- a kind of green structural adjustment . For the poorer nations , the obstacle is less political apathy than resource constraints . <p> Even when they try to prepare for the worst , they can not secure the resources needed to do the work properly . @@132191326 <h> Blind Spots in the Climate Movement <h> Share : <p> In the media and in activist circles , Climate Change is generally presented as a problem with one cause -- carbon emissions -- and one solution : a " green energy transition . " But this narrative is far too narrow , and unless we expand our collective perspective and responses , the already grievous consequences will worsen . <p> Many well-meaning people , some of whom dedicate much of their time and energy to the Climate Change cause , take part in disseminating this misleading narrative but I 'm not throwing shade on them at all . The narrative is so dominant it 's basically exclusive , and most people are unaware of anything else . My goal here is to broaden the discourse -- and the action we are taking -- by pointing out what I see as the big blind spots : a ) it 's not just carbon and b ) a " green " energy transition is not the only response . A third blind spot that relates to both is that " green @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some of which -- it must be emphasized -- are novel . <p> Blind Spot #1 : It 's not just carbon <p> Carbon emissions are certainly significant . I 'm not calling that into doubt . The greenhouse effect was first scientifically described in 1856 by Eunice Newton Foote . ( Of course a man coming to the same conclusion later was given the credit , &lt;eye roll&gt; . ) In the decades since then , we 've only learned more . <p> However , carbon emissions are only part of the story . The " other leg " is land use . In the literature , you 'll see various terms " land disturbance , " " land cover changes , " " land conversion " and " land alteration . " <p> Just as describing the full picture of carbon emissions is beyond the scope of essay , so is this subject , but I will sketch out the broad strokes here . <p> The term , " other leg , " is a nod to atmospheric scientist Millan Millan , of Spain , who described " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ leg for atmospheric carbon and the greenhouse effect , and a leg for land disturbance and hydrologic effects ( water cycles . ) " Here I 'm quoting Rob Lewis , who wrote a three-part series Substack about Millan 's important work , which can be found here , here and here . Rob 's series is so good I do n't mind if you go there now and forget to return to my words . <p> Land cover changes ( LCCs ) play an important role in the climate system . Research over recent decades highlights the impacts of these changes on atmospheric temperature , humidity , cloud cover , circulation , and precipitation . These impacts range from the local- and regional-scale to sub-continental and global-scale . It has been found that the impacts of regional-scale LCC in one area may also be manifested in other parts of the world as a climatic teleconnection . In light of these findings , this article provides an overview and synthesis of some of the most notable types of LCC and their impacts on climate . These LCC types include agriculture @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> That is , not only does climate affect agriculture , forests , deserts , cities , etc. , as is commonly discussed , but the converse is also true : agriculture , forests , deserts and cities affect the climate as well . Human alterations of the planet 's surface , especially major conversions like cutting down trees or draining wetlands or plowing under grasslands for farms , influence the atmosphere and water cycles both locally and at a wider scale . Considering the fact that as little as 3% of the earth 's ecosystems have not been disturbed by human activity , this is a really big deal . <p> Millan was inspired to study these relationships because the reliable afternoon summer rains of his childhood in Spain had become erratic and he wanted to know why . Quoting Rob again : <p> " Land-use perturbations ( mining , industrial and urban expansion , deforestation , paving ) that accumulated over historical time and greatly accelerated in the last 30 years " had rendered the land incapable of supporting the region 's climate , he determined . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vanishing , with far reaching implications for our understanding of the human causes of climate change and what we should do about it . my emphasis <p> Millan died in January 2024 , but he was not the only researcher pursuing these topics before or since . Also on Substack is Anastassia Makarieva , who runs " Biotic Regulation and Biotic Pump . " She also has a YouTube channel . She focuses on the relationship between ecosystems and water cycles , and hence climate . She writes : <p> In relation to the land 's water regime , biotic regulation takes the form of the biotic pump of atmospheric moisture . The biotic pump is a mechanism that operates in regions where forests are present ... The biotic pump ensures a controlled inflow of atmospheric moisture onto land ... Biotic regulation of moisture inflow occurs in various forms . During atmospheric moisture transport by cyclones , the intensity of the cyclone -- meaning the strength of the upward air movement and precipitation -- depends on the local concentration of water vapor in the atmosphere , which in turn depends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ atmospheric moisture levels , forests can regulate precipitation , triggering rain at the right time , in the right place , and in the quantity needed . Forests also shape specific soil properties , ensuring proper infiltration of moisture and regulating the turnover time of modern groundwater . <p> She often emphasizes on the vital role played by forests , and the necessity of protecting what remains . As someone who speaks for the trees , I greatly appreciate it . Reading her articles requires attention because her topics can be technical , but I highly recommend giving it a try . One of her more accessible pieces is " The Impending Catastrophe and How to Combat It . " ( Spoiler : we must safeguard all intact forests and restore degraded ones . ) <p> Though the work of both Millan and Makarieva is novel , it is not ground-breaking in the sense that they owe much to earlier researchers , something they both acknowledge . The study of how ecology affects weather and climate is not a new field , just an under-rated one . <p> We hear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , but the water cycle is just as important , if not more important in affecting the climate . How we use our land , what grows on it , how much our soils retain water , how much water the vegetation is transpiring into the air -- these things all affect the amount of water vapor in the air , which in turn affects rain patterns , droughts , and floods . The evaporation of water from vegetation also cools the land , transferring heat from ground level up into the clouds . Water acts as a regulator of heat on our planet , and as such plays a role in whether our planet cools or heats up . <p> Furthermore , it 's possible that human alteration of the environment led to climatic changes even before the Industrial Age and the use of fossil fuels . See " Did land-use and land-cover change affect Holocene climate ? " After all , as French philosopher Fran ? ois-Ren ? de Chateaubriand said , " Forests precede civilizations , and deserts follow them . Which raises the question : <h> Why do n't we hear much about " the other leg " ? <p> My personal take : Because the techno-industrial system can adapt itself -- or say it 's adapting itself -- to taking carbon emissions into account without fundamentally changing business-as-usual . For many years , we believed that Indian rivers were too mighty to fall , too sacred to collapse , and too eternal to disappear . But reality now tells a different story . These numbers are frightening because they show how deeply human behaviour , climate change , and moral neglect can damage something that once gave us life without asking anything in return . The rivers that carried our civilization for thousands of years are now carrying our waste , our chemicals , our untreated sewage , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change has made this decline sharper . Long droughts , weak monsoon rains , and rising temperatures have reduced the natural flow of many rivers . Scientific studies now reveal that the Ganga River is experiencing its lowest flow in more than a thousand years -- something unimaginable only a generation ago . Himalayan glaciers , which feed many northern rivers , are retreating . Snowfall is decreasing , and when snow does fall , it melts faster . When the sources of rivers weaken , the rivers lose their strength . India 's dependence on groundwater has further worsened the situation . Excessive pumping of water from the ground has reduced the natural recharge of riverbeds . When groundwater drops , rivers struggle , because many rivers actually flow from underground aquifers . These changes are slow , almost silent , but deeply destructive . <p> Alongside climate stress , human pressure has grown beyond what rivers can tolerate . Urban centres discharge untreated sewage into rivers daily . Industrial belts dump chemicals that poison fish and kill the smallest forms of life . Lakes and wetlands , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ being filled up or encroached upon . Sand mining has eaten into riverbeds , altering flow channels , deepening the beds , and increasing erosion along the banks . Dams and diversions have reshaped the natural movement of water . Floodplains , which once absorbed excess water and gave it back to rivers during dry months , are now covered with concrete , markets , colonies , and garbage . When all of this happens together -- pollution , mining , encroachment , climate stress -- the river begins to weaken from inside . Its flow reduces , its colour changes , its smell becomes unbearable , and its identity shrinks from a living river to a long wastewater drain . <p> This problem is not limited to the big rivers like Ganga , Yamuna , or Godavari . Even smaller rivers and Himalayan rivers such as the Jhelum are now showing signs of distress . The Jhelum River , once the lifeline of Kashmir , now carries large quantities of waste . Studies show that more than seventy percent of wastewater entering Jhelum remains untreated . Tributaries feeding the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which has been the spiritual starting point of the river for centuries , now faces the possibility of reduced flow if climate change continues to weaken winter snowfall . Pollution levels in certain stretches , especially near Srinagar , indicate that the river water is already contaminated by drainage , agricultural runoff , and solid waste dumping . Encroachments along the banks have narrowed the river . Excessive sand mining in the Jhelum basin threatens its natural shape and destroys its ecological balance . When a river like Jhelum , which depends on snow , springs , and small streams , begins to lose its sources , the danger becomes immediate . Unlike huge rivers that may still have large catchments , mountain rivers have very little margin . Once their sources suffer , the river quickly begins to shrink . <p> What makes this crisis even more profound is that it is not only a scientific or environmental issue . As Indians trade and transact with the rest of the world , money flows in and out of the country . The BoP shows how much money ( shown here in billions of US dollars ) went out of the country and how much money came in . All the money coming into the country is marked positive and all the money going out is marked negative . As such , in the BoP table , a minus sign points to a deficit . <p> -- The BoP matters because it captures the relative demand of the rupee vis- ? -vis the demand for foreign currencies ( represented in dollar terms ) . Hypothetically , if there were only two countries in the world , India and the US , every time an Indian wanted to buy an American good or service , or to invest in the US , they would have to hand over a certain number of rupees to first buy the dollars needed to complete that transaction . <p> -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by the relative demand of the two currencies -- if Indians demanded more dollars than Americans demanded rupees , the ' price ' ( or the exchange rate ) of the dollar relative to the rupee would go up . <p> Preliminary Examination : Current events of national and international importance <p> Mains Examination : General Studies-II : Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and issues arising out of their design and implementation . <p> What 's the ongoing story : The Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes ( Prevention ) Bill , 2025 , set to be introduced in the upcoming legislative session , proposes imprisonment ranging from two to 10 years for offenders and introduces the concept of collective liability for organisations . <p> Key Points to Ponder : <p> -- What are the laws against hate speech in India ? <p> -- What are cognisable offenses ? <p> -- What is Section 66A of the IT Act ? <p> -- What are the challenges in defining hate speech ? <p> -- Know about the 2018 Tehseen Poonawalla judgment <p> -- What are the necessary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Key Takeaways : <p> -- In the absence of a specific statute , Indian law enforcement agencies invoke a cluster of provisions from the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita to deal with cases involving hate speech . The Bill sought to define hate speech as any expression that " incites , justifies , promotes or spreads discrimination , hatred , hostility , or violence against a person or group . " <p> -- It also proposed to define " hate crime " as an offence motivated by prejudice against a victim 's real or attributed status , including religion , caste , gender identity or sexual orientation . <p> -- It proposed omitting Sections 153A and 295A of the IPC in favour of these more specific provisions , but it was not passed . <p> -- Karnataka is the first state in India to introduce a Bill specifically for targeting hate speech .
